Seat (104) resolves to none: the tasting is not organ-located; the whole self samples, not a faculty. Bearer (105) is the worshipper (inferred): the interior invited to sample God's goodness first-hand. Operation (106), the core event, is that the self invites others to taste and see that the LORD is good - trust made experiential, savoured rather than merely heard. Target (107) is experiential-trust (inferred): the aim is the first-hand savouring of God's goodness. Manner (108) is none - no mode is coloured. Intensity (109), specifier (110) and effect (111) are absent: no degree, no narrowing, no booked outcome - the reading rests on the invitation to taste. Coupling (112) is taste-and-see: the affect is welded to seeing, sampling and perceiving one movement. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: a summons to first-hand experience - the interior is to sample God's goodness, not just hear of it. Role (115) is characteristic - a standing trait. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state: the experiential trust is a condition of the inner being. The full process: from no named source and no organ-seat, the psalmist invites the interior to do more than hear about God - to taste and see that he is good, and so know his goodness first-hand - a movement of felt experience welded to seeing, held within as an inner state: trust here is not secondhand report but sampled reality, the blessed refuge of the next line grounded in a goodness actually tasted.
narratives.story: In the middle of this psalm comes one of its most famous invitations: taste and see that the Lord is good. It is a call to move past hearing about God to actually experiencing him. Trust here is not secondhand information but something you sample for yourself, the way you would taste food rather than just be told it is sweet. The psalmist wants his hearers to know God's goodness first-hand, to prove it on their own tongues. The passage does not argue it; it simply issues the invitation and pairs it with a blessing on the one who takes shelter in God. It is the warm, confident gesture of someone who has found God good and cannot merely describe it - who presses the cup toward others and says: try it yourself; you will find it is true.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'trust in the LORD and do good' - reliance joined to action. Type (102) is volition: an act of the will, trust commanded and coupled with doing, not a mere feeling. Source (103) is absent: the reading books no interior spring; the charge to trust simply stands, its origin unfiled. Seat (104) resolves to none: the trust is not organ-located; the whole self relies and acts, not a faculty. Bearer (105) is the hearer (inferred): the interior told not to fret over evildoers but to trust and do good. Operation (106), the core event, is that the self is told to trust in the LORD and do good, dwelling in the land and befriending faithfulness - reliance joined to action. Target (107) is active-trust (inferred): the aim is the reliance that works. Manner (108) is none - no mode is coloured. Intensity (109), specifier (110) and effect (111) are absent: no degree, no narrowing, no booked outcome - the reading rests on the commanded trust. Coupling (112) is trust-and-do-good: the volition is welded to doing good, reliance and action inseparable. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: the operation pairs an inner reliance with an outward doing; trust is not passive but works. Role (115) is characteristic - a standing trait. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state: the trust is a condition of the inner being. The full process: from no named source and no organ-seat, the hearer tempted to fret and envy the wicked is charged instead to trust the LORD and do good - a willed reliance welded to active doing and held within as an inner state: trust here is no folded-hands passivity but a settled leaning that expresses itself in going on doing good and befriending faithfulness while the evildoers fade like grass.
narratives.story: This psalm is written for people burning with frustration at how well the wicked seem to do. Its counsel is not just to feel differently but to act: trust in the Lord, and do good; dwell in the land and befriend faithfulness. Trust here is anything but passive. It is joined at the hip to doing good - the reliance shows itself in continuing to live well and faithfully instead of stewing over evildoers who will soon wither like grass anyway. The passage pairs the inner leaning with the outward life and refuses to separate them. It does not explain the trust further; it simply commands it alongside the doing. It is the down-to-earth picture of faith as something you both rest in and act on - trusting God with one hand while getting on with doing good with the other, rather than sitting still and fretting.
narratives.variation_note: Among the batach readings, this one is COMMANDED and ACTIVE (volition) - trust welded to 'do good,' reliance that works rather than folds its hands - directed to a fretting hearer, distinct from first-person trust in crisis. It stands beside the 'commit your way' charge of the same psalm (Psa 37:5).

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'commit your way to the LORD' - the rolling of one's whole road onto God. Type (102) is volition: an act of the will, a handing-over, not a mere feeling. Source (103) is absent: the reading books no interior spring; the charge simply stands, its origin unfiled. Seat (104) resolves to none: the committing is not organ-located; the whole self hands over, not a faculty. Bearer (105) is the hearer (inferred): the interior told to roll its way onto God and let him act. Operation (106), the core event, is that the self is told to commit its way to the LORD and trust him to act - handing over the whole course of life. Target (107) is entrustment (inferred): the aim is the surrender of one's road to God. Manner (108) is none - no mode is coloured. Intensity (109), specifier (110) and effect (111) are absent: no degree, no narrowing, no booked outcome - the reading rests on the committing. Coupling (112) is commit-your-way: the volition is welded to the act of rolling one's way onto God, surrender and reliance one. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: the rolling of one's road onto God - the interior lets go of managing outcomes and trusts him to work. Role (115) is characteristic - a standing trait. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state: the committing is a condition of the inner being. The full process: from no named source and no organ-seat, the hearer is charged to roll the whole course of his life onto the LORD - 'commit your way to the LORD; trust in him, and he will act' - a willed surrender welded to that handing-over and held within as an inner state: the interior stops trying to manage the result and lays the road itself in God's hands, trusting him to bring it about.
narratives.story: Set right next to the call to trust, this psalm adds a vivid instruction: commit your way to the Lord; trust in him, and he will act. The word behind commit pictures rolling a heavy load off your own shoulders and onto someone else's - here, rolling the whole course of your life onto God. It is a deliberate letting-go: the person stops trying to control how things turn out and hands the road itself over, trusting God to do the acting. The passage ties the committing straight to the promise that he will act. It does not analyse the inner move; it simply commands it. It is the freeing picture of a person who has been carrying the weight of managing his own future and finally sets it down where it belongs - rolling his path onto God and letting him carry it the rest of the way.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'they take refuge in him' - refuge as the ground of the whole deliverance. Type (102) is affect: a reliant movement, not a bare deed. Source (103) is absent: the reading books no interior spring; the sheltering simply stands as the reason for rescue, its origin unfiled. Seat (104) resolves to none: the refuge is not organ-located; the whole self shelters, not a faculty. Bearer (105) is the righteous (inferred): the interior of those the LORD helps and delivers from the wicked. Operation (106), the core event, is that the LORD helps and delivers the righteous from the wicked because they take refuge in him - refuge as the ground of rescue. Target (107) is refuge-taking (inferred): the aim is the sheltering itself. Manner (108) is none - no mode is coloured. Intensity (109), specifier (110) and effect (111) are absent: no degree, no narrowing, no booked outcome - the deliverance is read through the coupling, not filed as a separate effect. Coupling (112) is take-refuge: the affect is welded to the act of sheltering, made here the reason for the rescue. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: the operation closes the psalm on refuge - the whole deliverance of the righteous rests on their sheltering in God. Role (115) is characteristic - a standing trait. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state: the refuge is a condition of the inner being. The full process: from no named source and no organ-seat, the long psalm on the wicked's fading and the righteous' inheritance ends by tracing all the rescue to one cause - the LORD helps and delivers them because they take refuge in him - a reliant movement welded to the act of sheltering and held within as an inner state, refuge named as the very reason the righteous are saved.
narratives.story: This long psalm has watched the wicked draw their swords and the righteous quietly endure, promising that the evildoers will fade and the meek will inherit the land. At the very end it names the reason the righteous come through it all: the Lord helps them and delivers them from the wicked and saves them, because they take refuge in him. Everything traces back to that sheltering. Their rescue is not owed to their strength or their cleverness but to the fact that they have taken cover in God. The passage does not add anything further; it simply makes the refuge the ground of the whole deliverance. It is the closing note of a psalm about patience under injustice: the people who make it through are the ones who hid themselves in God, and that hiding is exactly why they are saved.
narratives.variation_note: The item H2620:takerefug (chasah, 'take refuge') runs across fifteen distinct readings in this family; readings 1-10 are coded as affect held as an internal ib-state, and 11-15 shift toward action/disposition whose locus is external, in God. This reading closes a long wisdom-psalm by making refuge the CAUSE OF RESCUE - the righteous are delivered 'because they take refuge in him' - shelter named as the ground of salvation, held as an inner state.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'my trusted friend has lifted his heel' - the wound of intimate betrayal, read from the side of the betrayed trust. Type (102) is affect: a movement of felt injury, not a bare deed. Source (103) is absent: the reading books no interior spring; the wound simply lands, its origin unfiled. Seat (104) resolves to none: the wound is not organ-located; the whole self is struck, not a faculty. Bearer (105) is the psalmist (inferred): the sick, whispered-against interior stabbed by one it had drawn closest. Operation (106), the core event, is that even the self's close friend, in whom it trusted, who ate its bread, has lifted his heel against it - the wound of intimate betrayal. Target (107) is betrayal (inferred): the aim, from the friend's side, is the betrayal; what registers in the psalmist is the injury of misplaced trust. Manner (108) is none - no mode is coloured. Intensity (109), specifier (110) and effect (111) are absent: no degree, no narrowing, no booked outcome - the reading rests on the wound. Coupling (112) is friend-lifts-heel: the affect is welded to that treacherous act, the trust and its betrayal one memory. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: the sharpest social wound - the interior is stabbed by the very one it had drawn closest and fed. Role (115) is characteristic - a standing trait of this suffering. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state: the wound is a condition of the inner being. The full process: from no named source and no organ-seat, the sick psalmist, surrounded by enemies wishing him dead, feels the deepest cut come not from them but from within his own circle - a close friend he had trusted and fed has turned on him - a felt injury welded to that betrayal and held within as an inner state: this is trust read at its point of rupture, the family's reliance shown in the pain of its violation.
narratives.story: Lying sick and surrounded by enemies who whisper about when he will die, the psalmist names the sharpest pain of all - and it does not come from his enemies. Even my close friend, he says, the one I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me. The deepest wound is a betrayal from inside his own circle: someone he had welcomed, fed, and leaned on has turned against him. It is the pain of trust broken by the very person it was given to. The passage does not soften it or explain the friend's reasons; it simply lets the injury stand at full weight. It is one of the loneliest lines in the Psalms - the discovery that the cruelty of strangers is easier to bear than the treachery of a friend, and that the closer the trust, the deeper the cut when it is betrayed.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is batach negated - 'not in my bow do I trust' - reliance disowned from weapons and given to God. Type (102) is action: a doing, an act of trusting, here in its negative form. Source (103) is absent: the reading books no interior spring; the disowning simply stands, its origin unfiled. Seat (104) resolves to none: the trust is not organ-located; the whole nation relies, not a faculty. Bearer (105) is the nation, the 'I' of the people (inferred): the collective interior that has boasted in God continually. Operation (106), the core event, is trust in its negated form - not the bow, not the sword. Target (107) is 'not my bow, but God' (inferred): the reliance is pointedly withheld from weapons and given to the God who saves. Manner (108) is none - no mode is coloured. Intensity (109), specifier (110) and effect (111) are absent: no degree, no narrowing, no booked outcome. Coupling (112) is none: uniquely the reading books no coupling - the trust stands stripped, defined only by what it refuses and where it lands. Prohibition (113) carries a value: the negation itself - 'NOT in my bow do I trust' - the reliance expressly forbidden to the weapon. Discovery (114) names it: reliance placed on God, not weapons - the same verb used elsewhere of trust in chariots, here disowned from bow and sword. Role (115) is characteristic - a standing trait. Locus (116) is external:god - the reference-point is set outside the self, in God who saves, not in the arm. The full process: from no named source and no organ-seat, the nation strips its reliance off its own weapons - not the bow, not the sword - and fixes it wholly outside itself in the God who has saved them from their foes; a trust defined by its prohibition and its external object, standing without any booked coupling, the confidence of a people who know their victories were never their arm's but God's.
narratives.story: Remembering how their ancestors won the land - not by their own sword or arm, but by God's right hand - this psalm draws the lesson for the present: for not in my bow do I trust, nor can my sword save me. The nation deliberately refuses to rest its confidence on its weapons. Trust here is defined by what it will not lean on: the bow is expressly ruled out, and the reliance is fixed instead entirely on God, who is the one who actually saves. There is nothing else propping it up - not strategy, not strength, just God. The passage strips the trust down to its bare truth. It is the picture of a people who have learned, from their own history, that their real security was never in the hardware of war but in the God who fought for them - and who say so plainly.
narratives.variation_note: Among the batach readings, this one is trust in its NEGATED form (action) - reliance forbidden to the bow and sword and located wholly outside the self in God (external:god), the one reading that books a prohibition and no coupling - kin to Psa 20:7 (chariots vs the name), distinct from the wealth-trust of the descent-readings.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is batach in its dark inversion - 'those who trust in their wealth' - reliance fixed on possessions. Type (102) is action: a doing, an act of trusting, here darkly misdirected. Source (103) is absent: the reading books no interior spring; the misplaced trust simply stands, its origin unfiled. Seat (104) resolves to none: the trust is not organ-located; the whole self of the rich relies, not a faculty. Bearer (105) is the rich who cheat (inferred): the interior of those whose iniquity surrounds the psalmist. Operation (106), the core event, is trust - the same reliance that elsewhere rests on God, here bent onto wealth. Target (107) is their wealth (inferred): the reliance is aimed at riches. Manner (108) is none - no mode is coloured. Intensity (109), specifier (110) and effect (111) are absent: no degree, no narrowing, no booked outcome - though the psalm shows wealth failing to ransom them from death, that ruin is not filed as this act's effect. Coupling (112) is a span-resolved pair - paired with boasting of their riches: the trust is welded to the boast, reliance and self-congratulation in wealth together. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names the inversion: misplaced confidence in possessions - batach, usually of trust in God, here the fool's reliance on wealth that cannot ransom him from death. Role (115) is characteristic - a standing trait of the rich. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the misplaced trust is a condition of the inner being. The full process, read at full weight in its descent: from no named source and no organ-seat, the rich cheaters lean their whole confidence on their wealth and boast of its abundance - the same reliance that ought to rest on God turned onto money - a trust welded to their boasting and lodged deep within as a settled state; and the psalm's verdict, though not filed as this act's effect, is that such wealth cannot buy off death: the confidence is real and it is doomed.
narratives.story: This psalm looks squarely at people who have staked everything on money - those who trust in their wealth and boast of the abundance of their riches. It uses the very word usually reserved for trusting God and turns it on its head: here it is reliance placed on possessions instead. Their trust and their boasting go together; they lean on their wealth and congratulate themselves on it. The passage does not flatter them because they are rich; it reads their confidence at full weight and then exposes its fatal flaw - no amount of money can ransom a life from death, and the wealthy die like everyone else, leaving it all behind. It is the sober picture of misplaced trust: people resting the whole weight of their security on something that feels solid and permanent but cannot follow them past the grave.
narratives.variation_note: Among the batach readings, this is a DESCENT-reading - the same verb, bent onto WEALTH by the rich who cheat, welded to boasting and lodged as an inner state - misplaced confidence in possessions that cannot ransom from death, the dark inversion of trust in God (contrast Psa 52:8; 62:8).

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is batach misdirected - 'trusted in the abundance of his riches' - the tyrant's fatal reliance on wealth. Type (102) is action: a doing, an act of trusting, here darkly misplaced. Source (103) is absent: the reading books no interior spring; the misplaced trust simply stands, its origin unfiled. Seat (104) resolves to none: the trust is not organ-located; the whole self of the tyrant relies, not a faculty. Bearer (105) is the tyrant (inferred): the interior of the boastful mighty man whose tongue plots destruction. Operation (106), the core event, is trust - reliance fixed on riches instead of God. Target (107) is a span-resolved pair - the abundance of his riches: the reliance is aimed squarely at wealth. Manner (108) carries a value: instead of making God his refuge (inferred) - the how is marked by contrast, the trust chosen in place of God. Intensity (109), specifier (110) and effect (111) are absent: no degree, no narrowing, no booked outcome. Coupling (112) is a span-resolved pair - the false trust set against the psalmist's trust in God (v8): the tyrant's reliance is welded in direct contrast to the true trust of the next verse. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: the fatal misplaced trust - reliance on wealth rather than God, the diagnosis of the tyrant's ruin, the exact counter to the psalmist who trusts God's steadfast love. Role (115) is characteristic - a standing trait of the tyrant. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the misplaced trust is a condition of the inner being. The full process, read at full weight in its descent: from no named source and no organ-seat, the boastful tyrant leans his whole confidence on the abundance of his riches - refusing to make God his refuge - a reliance welded as the exact opposite of the psalmist's trust in God's steadfast love, lodged deep within as a settled state: the reading names this misplaced trust as the very diagnosis of his coming ruin, the man uprooted precisely because he trusted his wealth and not God.
narratives.story: This psalm pronounces judgment on a powerful, boastful man whose words devour and whose tongue plots ruin, and it puts its finger on the root of his downfall. See the man, it says, who would not make God his refuge, but trusted in the abundance of his riches. His fatal mistake is named as a misplaced trust: he leaned his whole confidence on his wealth instead of on God. The passage sets this directly against the psalmist's own trust in God's steadfast love in the very next breath - the same act of trusting, aimed at opposite things, with opposite ends. It reads the tyrant's confidence at full weight and calls it his doom. It is the picture of a strong, rich man brought down not simply by his cruelty but by where he placed his trust - on money that could not save him, when he might have hidden in God.
narratives.variation_note: Among the batach readings, this DESCENT-reading is the tyrant's fatal trust in RICHES - explicitly 'instead of making God his refuge' and welded as the exact counter to the psalmist's trust in God's steadfast love (Psa 52:8) - misplaced confidence named as the diagnosis of ruin, paired in the same psalm with its opposite.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is azaz - 'grew strong / sought refuge in his own destruction' - the tyrant fortifying himself in his own ruin. Type (102) is action: a doing, an act of self-fortifying. Source (103) is absent: the reading books no interior spring; the self-securing simply stands, its origin unfiled. Seat (104) resolves to none: the operation is not organ-located; the whole self of the tyrant fortifies, not a faculty. Bearer (105) is the tyrant (inferred): the interior of the mighty man being uprooted. Operation (106), the core event, is to grow strong / seek refuge - the self making a stronghold of the wrong thing. Target (107) is a span-resolved pair - in his own destruction / greed: the strength is sought in his engulfing greed, the very thing that is his ruin. Manner (108) is none - no mode is coloured. Intensity (109), specifier (110) and effect (111) are absent: no degree, no narrowing, no booked outcome. Coupling (112) is a span-resolved pair - paired with trusting in riches: the self-fortifying is welded to the wealth-trust of the same verse, two faces of one misplaced security. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: the tyrant making his very ruin his stronghold - azaz to fortify oneself, here in engulfing greed rather than God, the self-securing that is itself the doom. Role (115) is characteristic - a standing trait of the tyrant. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the self-fortifying is a condition of the inner being. The full process, read at full weight in its descent: from no named source and no organ-seat, the tyrant makes himself strong not in God but in his own destroying greed - taking refuge in the very thing that destroys him - a self-fortifying welded to his trust in riches and lodged within as a settled state: this is refuge sought in exactly the wrong place, security built on the ground that is caving in, strength made of the self's own ruin.
narratives.story: Right beside the tyrant's trust in his riches, this psalm names a second, stranger move of his inner life: he sought refuge - made himself strong - in his own destruction. The word is one for fortifying oneself, building a stronghold; but the stronghold he builds is his own engulfing greed, the very thing that is ruining him. He takes cover in what destroys him. It is the exact opposite of taking refuge in God: instead of hiding in the one safe place, he fortifies himself on ground that is already collapsing. The passage ties this straight to his trust in wealth - the two are one misplaced security. It is a chilling picture of a person who thinks he is making himself safe while actually digging himself deeper into his own downfall - strength drawn from the very greed that will swallow him.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is batach rightly placed - 'I trust in the steadfast love of God forever' - the psalmist's answering trust. Type (102) is action: a doing, an act of trusting. Source (103) carries a real value, a span-resolved pair - resting on God's steadfast love (v8): uniquely among the nearby readings the origin is booked, the trust sourced in God's chesed. Seat (104) resolves to none: the trust is not organ-located; the whole self relies, not a faculty. Bearer (105) is the psalmist (inferred): the interior likened to a green olive tree in the house of God. Operation (106), the core event, is trust - reliance rightly placed on God. Target (107) is a span-resolved pair - the steadfast love of God: the reliance is aimed at God's chesed. Manner (108) carries a value, a span-resolved pair - forever and ever: the how is marked, a trust without end. Intensity (109), specifier (110) and effect (111) are absent: no degree, no narrowing, no booked outcome. Coupling (112) is a span-resolved pair - the true trust set against the tyrant's trust in riches (v7): this reliance is welded in direct contrast to the misplaced trust just condemned. narratives.story: Against the boastful tyrant who trusted his riches and is torn up by the roots, the psalmist sets his own answer: but I am like a green olive tree in the house of God; I trust in the steadfast love of God forever and ever. It is the same act of trusting the tyrant performed, but aimed at the opposite thing - not wealth, but God's faithful love - and meant to last forever. What makes this reading distinctive is that its source is named: the trust rests specifically on God's steadfast love, and its whole bearing is outward, toward God rather than toward anything in the self. The passage deliberately pairs the two men: one uprooted for trusting his money, the other flourishing like a well-rooted tree for trusting God. It is the picture of a life that endures precisely because of where it has placed its confidence.
narratives.variation_note: Among the batach readings, this ASCENT-reading is the deliberate COUNTER to the tyrant's wealth-trust in the same psalm (v7): it uniquely books its SOURCE (God's steadfast love), marks its manner 'forever,' and locates its locus external:god - trust rightly placed and enduring, the flourishing olive tree over against the uprooted strongman.

narratives.story: This psalm has been a storm of violence, treachery, and the special agony of betrayal by a close friend. It ends, though, on stillness. After naming the men of blood who will not live out half their days, the psalmist turns and says simply: but I will trust in you. It is the deliberate resting that closes all the turmoil - the last word, and it lands on God. Earlier the psalm had urged, cast your burden on the Lord, and he will sustain you; now the psalmist does exactly that, his trust answering that charge. His whole confidence is pointed outward, at God, and nowhere else. The passage does not resolve every wrong first; it simply lets the trust settle over the chaos. It is the picture of a man surrounded by violence and treachery who, instead of trusting his own defences, lays the whole weight of himself on God and rests.

narratives.story: This psalm keeps circling back to one line, and by verse eleven it reaches its highest point: in God I trust; I shall not be afraid. What can man do to me? Earlier the psalmist had trusted while still afraid; now, sure that God is for him, the trust has passed all the way into fearlessness. The same refrain he started with returns, but settled and confident, the dread fully answered. His whole reliance is fixed outward on God, and from that ground even his powerful attackers shrink to nothing. The passage does not explain the change beyond the assurance that God is on his side; it simply lets the refrain come to rest at its peak. It is the picture of trust that has done its work - a man once trembling now able to look at everyone who threatens him and ask, honestly, what can they really do?
narratives.variation_note: Among the batach readings, this is the trust-refrain of Psa 56 at its PEAK - restated after 'God is for me,' now marked by fearlessness (external:god) - the confidence that has passed through dread to rest, distinct from its first, fear-gripped statement at v3.

narratives.story: This is the first and most honest statement of the trust this psalm keeps repeating: when I am afraid, I put my trust in you. It does not pretend the fear is gone. The psalmist is being trampled and oppressed all day, and right in the grip of that dread he makes a deliberate choice to lean on God. Fear and trust are held together in the same breath - the trust is precisely what he does with his fear. And it rests on something named: the gracious God he appealed to at the very start of the psalm. The passage shows this as a move he will make over and over. It is the deeply relatable picture of faith not as fearlessness but as what you do when you are afraid - the decision, made in the middle of the terror, to put your weight on God anyway.
narratives.variation_note: Among the batach readings, this is trust CHOSEN INSIDE FEAR - 'when I am afraid, I put my trust in you' - the first statement of the Psa 56 refrain, uniquely booking its source (God's grace) and manner (in the moment of fear); it matures into the fearlessness of v4 and v11.

narratives.story: Just one verse after admitting that he trusts when he is afraid, the psalmist says it again - but something has shifted: in God, whose word I praise, in God I trust; I shall not be afraid. What can flesh do to me? The trust that a moment ago was gripped by fear has now grown into confidence. It is the same reliance on God, but matured - fear has given way to a kind of courage, and the enemies that loom so large are suddenly cut down to size. His whole trust is fixed on God, and from that footing human threats lose their teeth. The passage lets the trust visibly grow within a single psalm. It is the encouraging picture of what happens when you keep leaning on God through your fear: the leaning itself begins to steady you, until the thing you dreaded no longer seems able to touch you.
narratives.variation_note: Among the batach readings, this is the Psa 56 refrain MATURED - the trust of v3, chosen in fear, restated one verse later as settled fearless confidence ('what can flesh do to me?') - reliance grown into courage, and pointing on to the peak at v11 (external:god).

narratives.story: This psalm was written by a man hiding in a cave, on the run for his life. But the refuge he speaks of is not the cave. In you my soul takes refuge, he prays; be merciful to me. The deepest part of him flees not to the stone walls sheltering him but into God himself. Here, unusually, it is the very soul that takes cover - the shelter reaches right into the core of him - and it rests on God's mercy. He restates it at once in a vivid image: in the shadow of your wings I will take refuge, like a bird's young hiding under its mother. The passage does not treat the cave as his safety; it treats God as his safety. It is the picture of a hunted person who understands that the truest hiding-place is not a location at all but a person - and hides his soul in God.

Bearer (105) is the psalmist (inferred): the interior of the fugitive amid lions and fiery beasts. Operation (106), the core event, is to take refuge / shelter under God's wings. Target (107) is the shadow of God's wings (inferred): the sheltering is aimed under God's covering. Manner (108) carries a value - till the storms of destruction pass by (inferred): the how is marked, a patient hiding that waits out the storm. Intensity (109), specifier (110) and effect (111) are absent: no degree, no narrowing, no booked outcome. Coupling (112) is a span-resolved pair - the same refuge-taking, now under his wings: this reading is welded to the soul's refuge of the first clause, one flight twice named. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: the vivid image of sheltering under God like a bird's young - the deliberate, patient hiding until danger passes. The full process: from no separate source and no organ-seat, the fugitive, ringed by lion-like enemies, hides under God's wings and stays there till the storms of destruction pass by - a sheltering welded to the soul's refuge of the first clause, marked as patient waiting and located wholly external in God: refuge here is not a single dash to cover but a settled crouching beneath God's covering until the danger has spent itself.
narratives.story: Having said that his soul takes refuge in God, the psalmist paints the picture: in the shadow of your wings I will take refuge, till the storms of destruction pass by. It is the image of a small bird's young hiding under the outstretched wings of its mother while a storm rages outside. And notice the patience in it - he does not just duck under for a moment; he stays there until the danger has blown itself out. Surrounded by enemies he compares to lions and fiery beasts, he settles down under God's covering and waits. The passage does not promise the storm will not come; it promises a place to shelter until it goes. It is the tender, steadying picture of trust as crouching under God's protection through the worst of it - not a quick escape, but a patient hiding that outlasts the danger.
narratives.variation_note: See the variation note at Psa 57:1 (H2620:refug#1). This second reading restates the same flight under the WING-IMAGE and marks its manner as PATIENT WAITING - 'till the storms of destruction pass by' - refuge as a settled crouching under God's covering until danger passes (external:god), distinct from refug#1's seating in the soul.

Seat (104) resolves to none: the refuge is not organ-located; the whole self shelters, not a faculty. Discovery (114) names it: the sheltering in God's protective nearness, resting on the God who has already been his refuge and strong tower. Role (115) is characteristic - a standing trait. The full process: sourced in God's proven past protection and with no organ-seat, the faint-hearted psalmist, calling from far off, asks to hide under the shelter of God's wings - a sheltering welded to his longing to dwell in God's tent forever and located wholly external in God: because God has already been his refuge and strong tower, he asks to take permanent cover in that same nearness, trust grounded on a protection already tested.
narratives.story: Calling out from the end of the earth with his heart failing, the psalmist asks for two things that are really one: let me dwell in your tent forever, and let me take refuge under the shelter of your wings. He wants both to live near God and to hide under his covering, like a bird beneath its mother's wings. And his request is not a shot in the dark - it rests on experience. You have been my refuge, he says, a strong tower against the enemy. Because God has already proven himself a shelter, he asks to take cover there for good. The passage grounds the plea in the past even as it reaches for the future. It is the picture of a weary, far-off person longing to come home to God's protection - asking to stay under the wings that have already kept him safe before.
narratives.variation_note: This eleventh H2620:takerefug reading (chasah) marks the item's shift to ACTION with an external:god locus: sheltering under the wings, its source booked (God already his refuge and strong tower, v3) and welded to the longing to dwell in God's tent - trust grounded on protection already tested, distinct from the affect/inner-state readings 1-10.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is batach - 'put no trust in extortion' - reliance warned off ill-gotten gain. Type (102) is action: a doing, an act of trusting, here warned against. Seat (104) resolves to none: the trust is not organ-located; the whole self relies, not a faculty. Bearer (105) is the people, warned (inferred): the interior tempted to lean on plunder. Operation (106), the core event, is trust, wrongly - reliance the psalm warns the people against. Target (107) is a span-resolved pair - in extortion / robbery: the reliance is aimed at ill-gotten wealth. Manner (108) is none - no mode is coloured. Intensity (109), specifier (110) and effect (111) are absent: no degree, no narrowing, no booked outcome. Coupling (112) is a span-resolved pair - the misplaced counterpart to trusting God (v8), and to the heart set on riches: the warned trust is welded in contrast to the true trust urged two verses earlier. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: trust misdirected to ill-gotten gain - the same verb as trusting God, warned against when aimed at wealth won by force. Role (115) is characteristic - a standing trait. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the misplaced trust is a condition of the inner being. The full process, read at full weight in its descent: from no named source and no organ-seat, the people are warned off leaning their confidence on extortion and robbery, and off setting the heart on increasing riches - the same reliance that v8 urged toward God, here forbidden when it fastens on plunder - a misplaced trust welded as the exact counterpart to the trust in God just commanded, lodged as an inner state: the psalm exposes how easily reliance drifts from God onto stolen wealth, and calls it back.
narratives.story: Two verses after urging the people to trust in God at all times, this psalm turns to the counterfeit and warns them off it: put no trust in extortion; set no vain hopes on robbery; if riches increase, do not set your heart on them. It is the same act of trusting, but pointed the wrong way - at wealth, and specifically wealth won by force. The psalm knows how easily the heart slides from leaning on God to leaning on money, and it draws the two directly against each other. The passage does not soften the warning; it names the misplaced trust plainly and calls people back from it. It is the shrewd, honest picture of a temptation everyone feels - to let growing riches quietly become the thing you really rest on - and a firm reminder that such confidence, especially in gain got by cheating, is worth nothing.
narratives.variation_note: Among the batach readings, this is a DESCENT-warning - trust forbidden to extortion and robbery, welded as the misplaced counterpart to the trust in God urged two verses earlier (v8) - reliance drifting onto plunder, called back, distinct from the wealth-trust simply condemned in the wicked (Psa 49:6; 52:7).

Seat (104) resolves to none: the trust is not organ-located; the whole people relies, not a faculty. Bearer (105) is the people, exhorted (inferred): the interior called to lean on God in every season. Operation (106), the core event, is trust - reliance urged on all, at all times. Target (107) is God, at all times (inferred): the reliance is aimed at God in every season. Manner (108) carries a value - at all times (inferred): the how is marked, trust in prosperity and distress alike. Intensity (109), specifier (110) and effect (111) are absent: no degree, no narrowing, no booked outcome. Coupling (112) is a span-resolved pair - paired with pouring out the heart before God: the trust is welded to the pouring-out of the heart, reliance and unguarded openness together. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: the psalmist turning his own trust into an appeal to all - trust urged 'at all times' because God is a refuge, over against the vain trust in riches (v10). Role (115) is characteristic - a standing trait. Locus (116) is external:god - the reference-point is set outside the self, in God. The full process: sourced in God being a refuge and with no organ-seat, the psalmist widens his own settled trust into a call to everyone - 'trust in him at all times, O people; pour out your heart before him' - a reliance welded to that unguarded pouring-out, urged for every season and located external:god: because God is a refuge for all, the psalmist's private confidence becomes a public summons to lean on him always.
narratives.story: Having found God to be his own rock and salvation, the psalmist cannot keep the discovery to himself. He turns and calls everyone else in: trust in him at all times, O people; pour out your heart before him; God is a refuge for us. His private confidence becomes a public invitation. And notice the two things joined together - trusting God and pouring out your heart to him; the reliance goes hand in hand with unguarded honesty before him. The trust is meant for every season, good times and hard, and it rests on a simple reason: God is a refuge for all of us. The passage broadens one man's faith into a summons for the whole people. It is the warm picture of someone who has found God trustworthy and immediately wants others to lean on him too - at all times, holding nothing back.
narratives.variation_note: Among the batach readings, this one WIDENS private trust into a SUMMONS - 'trust in him at all times, O people' - booking its source (God is a refuge) and welding trust to pouring out the heart (external:god); it stands in the same psalm as its descent-counterpart, the warned trust in extortion (v10).

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is chasah - 'take refuge in him' - the righteous sheltering in God even as they rejoice. Type (102) is action: a doing, an act of taking shelter. Source (103) is absent: the reading books no interior spring; the sheltering simply stands, its origin unfiled. Seat (104) resolves to none: the refuge is not organ-located; the whole self shelters, not a faculty. Bearer (105) is the righteous (inferred): the interior of the upright in heart who exult. Operation (106), the core event, is to take refuge - shelter taken by the righteous in the moment of gladness. Target (107) is God (inferred): the sheltering is aimed at God. Manner (108) is none - no mode is coloured. Intensity (109), specifier (110) and effect (111) are absent: no degree, no narrowing, no booked outcome. Coupling (112) is a span-resolved pair - paired with rejoicing in the LORD: the refuge is welded to rejoicing, sheltering and gladness one movement. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114) names it: the refuge-taking that answers the psalmist's plea to be hidden (v2) - the safety the blameless find in God, who has shot down the ambushers. Role (115) is characteristic - a standing trait. Locus (116) is external:god - the reference-point is set outside the self, in God. The full process: from no named source and no organ-seat, the righteous, having watched God turn the ambushers' own tongues against them, both rejoice in the LORD and take refuge in him - a sheltering welded to that rejoicing and located external:god: the plea of the psalm's opening to be hidden from the secret plots is answered here, the blameless taking cover in the God who has just brought their hidden enemies to ruin.
narratives.story: This psalm began with a plea to be hidden from secret plots and the ambush of the wicked. By its close, God has turned the schemers' own tongues against them and brought them to ruin, and the righteous respond with two joined movements: let the righteous rejoice in the Lord and take refuge in him. They are glad and they take cover at the same time - the joy and the sheltering belong together. The safety they had prayed for at the start is now theirs, and they hide in the very God who dismantled their enemies. The passage ties the rejoicing and the refuge into one act. It is the picture of people who have watched God protect them and answer their fear, and who respond both by celebrating and by settling more deeply into him for cover - gladness and shelter as two sides of the same trust.

He opens it the same way he has apparently lived his whole life: in you, O Lord, do I take refuge; let me never be put to shame. This is no new discovery made in a crisis - it is the continuation of a lifetime of sheltering in God, who has been, as he says, his rock and fortress. And it rests on God's own righteousness to deliver and save. The passage shows an aging believer coming back, in his weakness, to the same cover that has kept him since youth. It is a moving picture of long faithfulness: a man near the end of his days, threatened and slandered, returning once more to the God he has always hidden in - not because it is new, but because it has always been true.

narratives.story: Growing old, the psalmist reaches for the one thing that has held steady through all his years: for you, O Lord, are my hope, my trust, O Lord, from my youth. His trust is not something new or a feeling that comes and goes; it is the settled ground his whole life has stood on, reaching all the way back to when he was young. Hope and trust are named together as the twin anchors of his existence. Now, weak and threatened, he leans on that same lifelong confidence rather than scrambling for a new one. The passage presents his faith as a fixed standing, not a fresh decision. It is the quietly powerful picture of someone at the far end of life who can say that the God he trusted as a young man is the very same God he is still trusting now - one unbroken reliance from youth to age.

His dependence on God goes back further than he can remember - before he was even aware of anything, God was already holding him up. His whole life has been one long leaning on God, a resting of his weight that started in the womb and never stopped. And out of that lifelong dependence flows a lifelong response: my praise is continually of you. The passage does not treat his faith as a choice he once made but as the very fabric of his existence. It is the moving picture of a person who realises that being upheld by God is not something he began but something he was born into - and whose natural answer, all his days, is unbroken praise.

narratives.story: This psalm nearly ended in disaster. Its writer confesses that he almost lost his footing, bitter and envious watching the wicked prosper - until he came into God's presence and saw how their story really ends. Now, on the far side of that crisis, he makes a firm decision about where his life will rest: I have made the Lord God my refuge. It is a deliberate choice, a settling of his whole security in God once and for all, after nearly settling it on the wrong thing. And the refuge has a purpose beyond safety - so that he may tell of all God's works. The passage shows shelter and testimony bound together. It is the picture of someone who came dangerously close to abandoning his faith, found his way back, and then planted his security in God so firmly that his life became a witness to it.

narratives.story: This psalm remembers a generation that had watched God do the impossible - split the rock so that water gushed out in the desert - and still would not believe him. They tested God, demanded the food they craved, and sneered, can he really give bread? And underneath it all was one failure: they did not trust his saving power. Here trust shows up by its absence. It is not that they trusted the wrong thing, but that they would not trust at all, withholding confidence from the very God who had just rescued them. The passage reads that missing trust at full weight and names it as what kindled God's anger. It is the sobering picture of unbelief as a settled refusal - people with every reason to rely on God who simply would not, and whose hardened distrust is presented as their real sin.

narratives.story: This psalm shows God standing up in the council of the mighty and putting the powerful on trial with a single accusation: how long will you judge unjustly and show partiality to the wicked? The charge is favouritism - lifting up the face of the guilty because they are strong, tilting justice toward those with power and against the weak, the fatherless, the destitute. It is not a one-off lapse but a settled bent inside the judges, a will already leaning toward the wicked before any case is heard. The passage reads that inner tilt at full weight and God condemns it outright, sentencing these 'gods' to die like men. It is the unflinching picture of corrupted justice from the inside - officials whose hearts are quietly sold to the powerful, and a God who arraigns them precisely for that hidden partiality.

narratives.story: This is a psalm of homesickness for God - a soul fainting for his courts, envying even the sparrow that gets to nest at his altar, a pilgrim making the long journey to appear before him. All of that yearning comes to rest in the very last line: O Lord of hosts, blessed is the one who trusts in you. The longing does not stay restless; it resolves into a settled trust. The happy person, the psalm concludes, is simply the one who leans on God. It is not a single act but a whole bearing of life, and it is pointed entirely at God. The passage lets all its ache and travel land on this quiet confidence. It is the satisfying picture of desire finding its home - a heart that has longed and journeyed for God finally settling into the plain, blessed trust that he is enough.

narratives.story: This is a prayer from someone poor and needy, crying to God all day long, and near the start he names the ground he stands on: preserve my life, for I am godly; save your servant, who trusts in you - you are my God. His trust is not one item on a list of requests; it is the settled bearing underneath everything he asks. He leans on God, and that leaning is why he expects to be heard. The reliance and his devotion to God go together. The passage does not analyse the trust; it simply lets it undergird the whole prayer. It is the plain, humble picture of a person in need who approaches God not with achievements but with dependence - offering, as his one credential, that he is someone who trusts, and asking God to act on the strength of that.

narratives.story: This famous psalm of protection opens by naming where its whole confidence comes from. I will say to the Lord, the psalmist declares, my refuge and my fortress, my God, in whom I trust. Trust and shelter are spoken in the same breath - to call God his refuge is, in the same movement, to say he trusts him. It is a settled bearing, not a one-time act, and it points entirely outward to God. Everything that follows - the promise of rescue from the fowler's snare and the deadly plague, the covering wings, the shield of faithfulness - rests on this opening reliance. The passage plants the trust first and builds the assurances on top of it. It is the picture of a person whose deep sense of safety is not free-floating optimism but a confidence anchored in God, named plainly at the outset as the ground of it all.

narratives.story: Alongside naming his trust, the psalmist names his shelter, and the two are really one confession: I will say to the Lord, my refuge and my fortress. To call God his refuge is to say out loud where his safety actually lives - not in himself, not in any defence of his own, but in God. It is a settled way of seeing, not a passing feeling, and it points entirely outward. Shelter and trust are declared in the same breath, twin sides of the same confidence. The passage makes this confession the foundation of the psalm's sweeping promises of protection. It is the picture of a person who has decided, once and for all, that God himself is the fortress he lives in - and who founds everything else on simply saying so.

narratives.story: At the heart of this psalm of protection is one of the tenderest images in the Bible: he will cover you with his pinions, and under his wings you will find refuge. The person who trusts God is pictured as a small bird sheltering beneath its mother's outstretched wings - hidden, warmed, kept. Taking refuge here is simply running to that covering. And the psalm adds that God's own faithfulness is a shield and buckler around him, so the soft image of wings and the hard image of armour meet in one protection. The passage turns what elsewhere is a fugitive's desperate prayer into a settled promise. It is the reassuring picture of trust as nestling under God - not braced and exposed, but tucked safely beneath a covering that is at once gentle as feathers and strong as a shield.

Worship here is not only something felt but something carried - the inner honouring of God takes the form of an actual gift brought into his presence. The families of the nations are summoned to turn toward God and come to him bearing something. The passage joins the inward ascribing of glory to the outward act of bringing, so that the two are one movement. It is the picture of reverence that will not stay abstract - a heart so turned toward God that it walks into his courts with a gift in hand, letting the offering say what the worship means.

narratives.story: This psalm of a man crushed by his accusers turns for a moment to his own body, and the picture is of someone wasting away. My knees are weak through fasting, he says; my body has become gaunt, with no fat. Worn down by sorrow and long fasting, he is physically hollowing out - thin, weak, emptied. And it is tied to what is happening inside him: he is an object of scorn, mocked by those who see him, and the wasted body is the outward mark of that inward affliction. The passage does not explain or relieve it; it simply shows a sufferer thinned to skin and bone by grief. narratives.story: This psalm portrays the settled, blessed life of the person who fears God, and it puts its finger on what keeps such a person steady: he is not afraid of bad news; his heart is firm, trusting in the Lord. When alarming reports come - the kind that would make anyone's stomach drop - his heart does not lurch, because it is anchored. The trust is a settled bearing, not a one-time act, and it is fixed entirely on God. What the passage highlights is the steadiness it produces: a heart so firmly held that it can wait calmly, even look in eventual triumph on its enemies. It does not explain the trust further; it simply shows the calm it creates. It is the enviable picture of a person whose inner life is not at the mercy of the next piece of frightening news, because it rests on something steadier than circumstances.

narratives.story: Having just mocked the idols of the nations - gods with mouths that cannot speak, eyes that cannot see, hands that cannot feel - this psalm turns and calls God's people to lean somewhere real: O Israel, trust in the Lord! He is their help and their shield. It is a summons to true trust, set in sharp contrast to the dead things the surrounding peoples rely on. The living God can actually help and protect; the idols can do nothing. This is the first of three such calls in a row, addressed to the whole nation. The passage urges a settled bearing of reliance, pointed entirely at God. It is the bracing picture of a people being called off worthless securities and onto the one that holds - told plainly to put their trust where there is genuine help and a genuine shield.

narratives.story: The call to trust widens. Having summoned all Israel, the psalm now turns to the priests: O house of Aaron, trust in the Lord! He is their help and their shield. Even those who serve at the altar, closest to the sacred rites, are told to lean not on their sacred office but on God himself. The summons is the same as to the nation - trust the living God, who alone gives real help and protection - now pressed on the priestly house in particular. It is a settled bearing being urged, pointed entirely at God. The passage refuses to let anyone, however religious their role, rest on something other than God. It is the pointed picture of a call to trust that reaches even the professionally holy - reminding the priests that their security, like everyone's, lies not in what they do but in the God they are called to lean on.

narratives.story: The threefold call reaches its widest here: you who fear the Lord, trust in the Lord! He is their help and their shield. Beyond the nation and beyond the priests, the summons now gathers everyone who reveres God at all and presses them onto him. And notice how trust and the fear of God are joined: reverence for God completes itself in reliance on him. To fear God rightly is, in the same movement, to lean on him. The reliance is a settled bearing, pointed entirely outward at God. The passage will not let the fear of God stay a mere awe; it turns it into trust. It is the gathering picture of everyone who takes God seriously being cast wholly on him - told that the proper response to revering God is not to keep a nervous distance but to put your full weight on him as your help and shield.
narratives.variation_note: Among the batach readings, this is the THIRD and widest of Psa 115's summons - all God-fearers cast on him, trust twinned with the fear of God (external:god) - reverence completing itself in reliance, distinct from the nation (v9) and priest (v10) calls and from the descent idol-trust of v8.

The full process, read at full weight in its descent: from no named source and no organ-seat, those who make idols - mouths that cannot speak, eyes that cannot see - and trust in them become like them, hollowed out to match the deadness they rely on - a misplaced disposition bound to an inner deadening and paired with the very making of the images: here the family's trust is read at its most futile and self-destructive, reliance on nothing that empties the one who relies, so that the truster takes on the lifelessness of what he trusts.
narratives.story: Right before the calls to trust the living God, this psalm delivers a chilling verdict on the alternative. After describing idols that cannot speak, see, hear, or feel, it says: those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them. Trusting dead things does something terrible to the one who trusts - it hollows him out to match them. The idolater takes on the very lifelessness of the images he relies on. It is a settled bearing bent toward nothing, and it deadens from the inside. The passage reads this misplaced trust at full weight, not as a harmless mistake but as self-destruction. It is the stark picture of what reliance on empty things does to a person: you become like what you trust, and to trust in the lifeless is to grow lifeless yourself - the exact opposite of the living help and protection God offers.

narratives.story: Out of his own rescue - I called on the Lord, and he answered me and set me free - the psalmist draws a plain comparison: it is better to take refuge in the Lord than to trust in man. Trusting people is not condemned as wicked here; it is simply weighed against trusting God and found to be the weaker ground. Human help lets you down; God does not. The reliance on man is a settled tendency of the heart, and the passage measures it against sheltering in God and finds it wanting. It is the down-to-earth wisdom of someone who has learned the difference by experience - who knows how easily we lean on people, princes, powers, and how much surer it is to hide in God instead. Better, he says, to take refuge in the Lord.

narratives.story: The same comparison, read from the bright side: it is better to take refuge in the Lord than to trust in man. Where the previous line weighed human help and found it wanting, this one names the winner outright - taking cover in God is simply the better ground. The psalmist, freshly rescued after calling on God, states it as settled conviction: of the two places a person might put his weight, God is the wiser choice. It is a bearing of life, not a one-off decision, and it points entirely at God. The passage sets shelter in God directly against reliance on man and comes down firmly on the side of the refuge. It is the confident wisdom of experience - a person who has tried calling on God and found him faithful, and now recommends, plainly, that this is the smarter place to hide.

Even the powerful - rulers with armies and wealth, the strongest help a person could hope for - are a weaker ground than God. Trusting them is not evil, just unreliable when measured against sheltering in God. It is a settled leaning of the heart, and the passage weighs it and finds it wanting. It is the hard-won wisdom of someone who knows how tempting it is to pin your hopes on the mighty, and who insists that even the greatest human power is a poorer refuge than God himself.
